'''Luigi Di Lella''' (born in Naples, 7 December 1937) is an Italian [[Experimental particle physics|experimental particle physicist]]. He has been a staff member at [[CERN]] for over 40 years, and has played an important role in major experiments at CERN such as [[CERN Axion Solar Telescope|CAST]] and [[UA2 experiment|UA2]]. From 1986 to 1990 he acted as spokesperson for the UA2 Collaboration, which, together with the [[UA1 experiment|UA1 Collaboration]], discovered the [[W and Z bosons]] in 1983.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://home.cern/about/updates/2013/01/carrying-weak-force-thirty-years-w-boson |title=Carrying the weak force: Thirty years of the W boson |last=O'Luanaigh |first=Cian |date=12 March 2015 |website=cern.ch |publisher=CERN |access-date=24 July 2017}}</ref>

==Education==
After moving from his child-hood home in Naples, Italy, Di Lella studied physics at the [[University of Pisa]] and [[Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa|Scuola Normale Superiore in Pisa]]. Di Lella obtained his doctoral degree in 1959 from the University of Pisa on the subject of [[muon capture]]. Written under the supervision of [[Marcello Conversi]], his thesis was on the measurement of longitudinal polarization of [[neutrons]] emitted from [[muon capture]] in [[Atomic nucleus|nuclei]] (in Italian, unpublished).

==Career and research==
Following his degree, Di Lella continued his work with Marcello Conversi, now at the [[Sapienza University of Rome|University of Rome]]. He was commuting between Rome and CERN, using the [[Synchro-Cyclotron (CERN)|Synchrocyclotron]] at CERN as an accelerator for his experiments, before he in 1961 secured a two-year position as a Fellow at CERN.

In the 1950s physicist had started to wonder why processes like the decay of a positive [[muon]] to a [[positron]] and a [[photon]], {{math|''μ''<sup>+</sup>→''e''<sup>+</sup> + ''γ''}}, or [[electron emission]] from nuclear capture of a negative muon, {{math|''μ''<sup>−</sup> + N → N + ''e''<sup>−</sup>}}, were not observed. Given the knowledge of that time, there was no reason why these reactions could not exist – [[Conservation of energy|energy]], [[Charge conservation|charge]] and [[Spin (physics)|spin]] are conserved. Di Lella took part in two consecutive experiments with increased sensitivity on the search for electron emission from nuclear capture of negative muons, strengthening the hypothesis that muon and electron have different quantum number (today named [[Flavour quantum numbers|"lepton flavour"]]).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Conversi |first1=M. |last2=Di Lella |first2=L. |last3=Penso |first3=G. |last4=Rubbia |first4=C. |last5=Toller |first5=M. |date=1 February 1962 |title=Search for Conversion of Muons Into Electrons |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/343734/files/PhysRevLett.8.125.pdf?version=1 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=8 |issue=3 |pages=125–128 |doi= 10.1103/PhysRevLett.8.125|access-date=24 July 2017 |bibcode=1962PhRvL...8..125C }}</ref> The definitive experimental proof of this hypothesis was achieved in 1962 in the first high-energy neutrino experiment at the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory|Brookhaven]] 30 GeV [[Alternating Gradient Synchrotron]] ('''AGS'''), by showing that neutrinos from {{math|''π''<sup>+</sup>→''μ''<sup>+</sup> + ''ν''}} only produced muons, and not electrons, when interacting in the detector, a result for which [[Leon Lederman]], Mel Schwartz and [[Jack Steinberger]] shared the 1988 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Danby |first1=G. |last2=Gaillard |first2=J. M. |last3=Goulianos |first3=Konstantin A. |last4=Lederman |first4=L. M. |last5=Mistry |first5=Nari B. |last6=Schwartz |first6=M. |last7=Steinberger |first7=J. |date=1 July 1962 |title=Observation of High-Energy Neutrino Reactions and the Existence of Two Kinds of Neutrinos |url=http://inspirehep.net/record/28187 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=9 |issue= 1|pages=36–44 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.9.36 |access-date=24 July 2017|bibcode=1962PhRvL...9...36D |url-access=subscription |hdl=2027/mdp.39015095280841 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1988/press.html |title=About the Nobel Prize in Physics 1988 |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=19 October 1988 |website=Nobelprize.org |access-date=24 July 2017 }}</ref>

From 1964 to 1968 Di Lella held a position as a Research Physicist at CERN. During this time he took part in experiments at the [[Proton Synchrotron]] (PS), on high-energy [[elastic scattering]] of [[hadrons]] from [[polarized target]]s, discovering unexpected spin effects in the diffractive region, with opposite sign for {{math|''π''<sup>+</sup>}} and {{math|''π''<sup>−</sup>}}.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Borghini |first1=M. |last2=Dick |first2=L. |last3=Di Lella |first3=L.|display-authors=etal|date=16 March 1970 |title=Measurement of the polarization parameter in pi+- p, k+- p, p p, and anti-p p elastic scattering at 6 gev/c |url=https://inspirehep.net/record/63191 |journal=Physics Letters B |volume=31 |issue=6 |pages=405–409 |doi=10.1016/0370-2693(70)90208-X |access-date=24 July 2017|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The following year, Di Lella became an Associate Professor of Physics at [[Columbia University]], New York, a position he held for two years, until 1970.

After receiving an offer from CERN for an indefinite appointment as a Research Physicist, Di Lella returned to CERN in 1970. The construction of the [[Intersecting Storage Rings]] (ISR) at CERN, the world's first [[hadron collider]], had recently been completed. While still at Columbia University, Di Lella, together with physicists from CERN, Columbia and [[Rockefeller University]], wrote a proposal for an ISR experiment to search for high-mass electron-positron pairs.<ref name=R103>{{cite journal |last1=Cool |first1=R. |last2=Di Lella |first2=L. |last3=Lederman |first3=L. |last4=Zavattini |first4=E. |date=20 June 1969 |title=Preliminary Proposal: Intersecting Storage Rings Study of Dileptons |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1005387/files/CM-P00062888.pdf |journal=IRS Committee |access-date=24 July 2017}}</ref> The experiment, known as R-103, had two large detectors at 90 degrees to the beam directions at opposite [[azimuth]] angles, to detect electrons, positrons and photons and to measure their energies and angles.<ref name=R103/> It soon found an unexpected high rate of high-energy photons from the [[Pion#Neutral pion decays|decay of neutral mesons]] ({{math|''π''<sup>0</sup>}}) emitted at large angles to the beams.<ref name=Busser>{{cite journal |last1=Büsser |first1=F. W. |last2=Camillieri |first2=L. |last3=Di Lella |first3=L.|display-authors=etal|date=18 February 1974 |title=A search for large transverse momentum electrons at the CERN ISR |journal=Physics Letters B |volume=48 |issue=4 |pages=371–376 |doi=10.1016/0370-2693(74)90611-X |bibcode=1974PhLB...48..371B }}</ref> Because in the early 1970s there were no high-capacity [[hard disks]], nor sophisticated [[Data acquisition|data acquisition systems]], data were written onto [[magnetic tapes]] at a rate that could not exceed 10 events per second (even so, a magnetic tape became full after 15 minutes of data taking). To keep the event rate below this limit, the electron detection threshold used in the event trigger was raised above 1.5 GeV, thus excluding from detection the yet undiscovered [[J/psi meson|{{math|''J''/''Ψ''}}-particle]] with 3.1 GeV mass<ref name=Busser/> (this particle, a [[bound state]] of a [[charm quark|charmed quark-antiquark]] pair, was discovered in 1974 at the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory|Brookhaven]] AGS and at the electron-positron collider [[SPEAR]] at [[Stanford]], and for this discovery the 1976 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] was awarded to [[Burton Richter|B. Richter]] and [[Samuel Chao Chung Ting|S.C.C. Ting]]).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1976/ |title=The Nobel Prize in Physics 1976 |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=18 October 1976 |website=Nobelprize.org |access-date=24 July 2017 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Augustin |first1=J. E.|display-authors=etal|date=2 December 1974 |title=Discovery of a Narrow Resonance in e+e− Annihilation |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=33 |issue=23 |pages= 1406–1408|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.33.1406 |bibcode=1974PhRvL..33.1406A|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Aubert |first1=J. J.|display-authors=etal|date=2 December 1974 |title=Experimental Observation of a Heavy Particle J|journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=33 |issue=23 |pages= 1406–1408|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.33.1406 |doi-access=free |bibcode=1974PhRvL..33.1406A }}</ref>

The production of high-energy {{math|''π''<sup>0</sup>}} mesons at large angles was soon understood as due to the [[strong interaction]] of point-like constituents of the proton (quarks, antiquarks and [[gluons]]). Evidence for electrically charged, point-like proton constituents, [[electromagnetic interaction|interacting electromagnetically]] with electrons, had already been found in 1968 at the [[Stanford Linear Collider]] at [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|SLAC]] from deep-inelastic electron scattering experiments, for which [[Jerome Isaac Friedman|J. Friedman]], [[Henry Way Kendall|H. Kendall]] and [[Richard E. Taylor|R. Taylor]] received the 1990 Nobel Prize in Physics 1990.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1990/press.html |title=Press Release: The 1990 Nobel Prize in Physics |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=17 October 1990 |website=Nobelprize.org |access-date=24 July 2017 }}</ref> The R-103 experiment found that these constituents behaved as point-like particles also when interacting strongly.<ref name=R103/>

The R-103 results were in contrast with earlier theories of proton-proton collisions, which predicted that only low-energy [[mesons]] would be produced at large angles. The experiment was a step towards understanding the strong interaction between hadron constituents. Unfortunately, the discovery of high-energy {{math|''π''<sup>0</sup>}} meson production at large angle prevented the more important discovery of the {{math|''J''/''Ψ''}}-particle.

In 1978 Di Lella was one of four senior physicist who proposed the [[UA2 experiment]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Banner |first1=M|display-authors=etal|date=31 January 1978 |title=Proposal to Study Antiproton-Proton Interactions at 540 GeV CM Energy |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/596804/files/CM-P00045649.pdf |journal=SPS Committee |access-date=24 July 2017}}</ref> The purpose of the experiment was to detect the production and decay of the [[W and Z bosons]] at the [[Proton-Antiproton Collider]] ('''Sp{{overline|p}}S''') — a modification of the [[Super Proton Synchrotron]] ('''SPS'''). UA2, together with the [[UA1 experiment|UA1 collaboration]], succeeded in discovering these particles in 1983, leading to the 1984 Nobel Prize in Physics being awarded to [[Carlo Rubbia]] and [[Simon van der Meer]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1984/press.html |title=Press Release: The 1984 Nobel Prize in Physics |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=17 October 1984 |website=Nobelprize.org |access-date=24 July 2017 }}</ref> UA2 was also the first experiment to observe [[Jet (particle physics)|hadronic jet]] production at high transverse momentum from hadronic collisions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=UA2 Collaboration |date=2 December 1982 |title=Observation of very large transverse momentum jets at the CERN ppbar collider |journal=Phys. Lett. B |volume=118 |issue=1–3 |pages=203–210 |doi=10.1016/0370-2693(82)90629-3 |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/139969/files/198210291.pdf |bibcode=1982PhLB..118..203B }}</ref> Di Lella was the spokesperson of the UA2 experiment from 1986 to 1990, when high-luminosity operation of the Sp{{overline|p}}S was discontinued.

During the 1990s Di Lella became interested in [[neutrino oscillations]]. He was among the proponents of the WA96/NOMAD experiment, which aimed at searching for ν<sub>μ</sub>-ν<sub>τ</sub> oscillations using high-energy neutrinos (predominantly ν<sub>μ</sub>) from the CERN SPS, and he became the spokesperson for the experiment in 1995.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Astier |first1=P.|display-authors=etal|date=11 March 1991 |title=Proposal: Search for the Oscillation {{math|''ν''<sub>μ</sub>→''ν''<sub>τ</sub>}} |url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/294919/files/SC00000435.pdf |journal=SPS Committee |access-date=24 July 2017}}</ref> Guided by a theoretical conjecture that the [[Tau neutrino|3rd neutrino]] might be the main component of [[dark matter]] in the Universe, they looked for oscillations over an average distance of ~650 m. They found no oscillations, and when these oscillations were first observed by the [[Super-Kamiokande|Super-Kamiokande experiment]] in Japan using neutrinos produced by [[cosmic rays]] in the Earth atmosphere, they were found to occur over distances of the order of 1000&nbsp;km ([[Takaaki Kajita|T. Kajita]] and [[Arthur B. McDonald|A. McDonald]] shared the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery of neutrino oscillations).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2015/press.html |title=Press Release: The 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=6 October 2015 |website=Nobelprize.org |access-date=24 July 2017 }}</ref>

From 2000 until his retirement Di Lella took part in the [[CERN Axion Solar Telescope|CAST]] experiment (CERN Axion Solar Telescope experiment), searching for [[axions]] produced in the core of the Sun. After retiring in 2004, Di Lella has been a research associate in the schools where he did his first strides as a physicist: Scuola Normale Superiore in Pisa and University of Pisa. He is still actively working at CERN, doing experiments on charged [[K-meson]] decay at the [[NA62 experiment]].

From 1991 to 2006 Di Lella was a supervisory editor if the journal [[Nuclear Physics B]].
